title: One last offer of peace
hookLine: Lanka surrounded at four gates, and still Rama sends Angada with an offer of peace

cards: Rama climbs Mount Suvela with his leaders to look at Lanka. And there, on a high tower across the way, stands Ravana himself, in royal clothes, among his attendants. Sugriva can't stand it.
Without a word to anyone he leaps across, lands on the tower, knocks off Ravana's crown, and the two kings wrestle. Then Sugriva jumps back, pleased with himself. Rama is not pleased.
A king doesn't do that, he says. If something had happened to you, what would I have done?

teach.b: Then Rama does things in order.

Lanka has four great gates, and he assigns a leader to each: Nila to the east, Angada to the south, Hanuman to the west, and Rama himself, with Lakshmana, to the north, where Ravana is. The city is surrounded.

And still, before the first blow, Rama sends a messenger: Angada, Vali's son. Angada leaps to Ravana's palace and speaks plainly: return Sita, ask pardon, and you'll live. If not, Vibhishana will rule Lanka.
Ravana orders him seized. Four rakshasas grab him by the arms. Angada springs onto the palace roof with all four hanging on; they drop off, he breaks the roof's peak, and leaps back to Rama.
You may know a later scene from Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas, Angada's foot planted in Ravana's court that no one can lift. In Valmiki it's the broken rooftop. Here's the teaching underneath.
Old Hindu teaching on kingship names four ways to settle a conflict: sama, talking and making peace; dana, giving; bheda, splitting the other side; and danda, force. Force comes last.
Hanuman weighs all four in Lanka before he fights, and the Mahabharata shows it on a bigger stage: before Kurukshetra, Krishna himself goes to the Kauravas' court to ask for peace.
So Rama, with every gate covered, still starts with sama. Only after Angada returns does the battle begin. Today, most sieges are smaller: a family feud, a friend group split in two.
Sama first means the plain offer of peace comes before anything else, even when you could win.

how: In North Indian Ramlila performances, Angada's embassy to Ravana's court is a well-known scene, often played in the Ramcharitmanas version with Angada's unmovable foot.

o: Lanka ringed at four gates, with one last offer of peace
a long truce while Ravana thinks over Rama's offer
a surprise attack on Lanka before any warning

carried the last offer of peace

s: in Valmiki, Angada plants his foot and no one can lift it
that's from later tellings like the Ramcharitmanas; Valmiki has him break the rooftop.
Rama offers peace even after Lanka is surrounded
Angada carries the offer: return Sita, and live.
Rama praises Sugriva for wrestling Ravana
he tells him a king shouldn't take such a risk alone.

games.q: your friend group has split over a fight, and you could rally everyone to your side. by the Hindu teaching of the four means, where do you start?
o: sama: a plain, honest offer to make peace.
bheda: quietly pull their friends away first.
danda: hit back hard so it ends fast.
games.why: sama comes first and danda, force, comes last. even with Lanka surrounded, Rama sent Angada to offer peace.

practice: Sit tall and bring to mind a conflict you're in, at home or at work. Many Hindu prayers end with one word said three times, shanti: peace. On three slow out-breaths, say it softly, shanti, shanti, shanti.
Then hold one quiet question: have I made a plain offer of peace? If you don't pray, breathe the word anyway and keep the question.

wordCard.voice: The siege. Lanka's four gates surrounded, and still, sama first: one last offer of peace, carried by Angada before the first battle.

orig.note: Sanskrit Aṅgada: Vali's son; the word also names an armlet, an ornament worn on the upper arm.

carryVoice: Your line: sama first, peace before force. The war's first night is coming. That's day six hundred forty.
